whyThisMatters: A lot of what feels true about staying safe offshore is only partly right — and limited time online makes it harder to pause and check when a rotation link, a call, or a request already sounds routine. A few minutes here will clear up what really matters when a message already looks familiar.
rememberThis: This month's reminder: familiar packaging is not proof. A rotation email, a confident-sounding caller, or an urgent fund request can all be faked — verify through the portal you already use or a number you already have, every time.

discussionPrompts: Ask how much slower it actually is to press and hold a link before tapping it, versus the risk of tapping a fake one.
For the USB-stick myth, ask what people would actually do if they found one on the bridge right now.
Ask the group to describe their own trusted way to verify an urgent call or text with limited time online.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often get the phone-call myth wrong. A caller who sounds official and uses the right internal terms feels trustworthy, so many people say it's fine to answer their questions. But a voice and correct terminology can both be faked — hanging up and calling back on a known number is the only real check.

items.myth: A rotation or crew-portal link is safe to tap as long as the blue text shows the correct address.
items.fact: The visible text of a link can say anything — only pressing and holding it (or hovering on a computer) reveals where it actually goes, which is the only real check.
items.detail: Limited time online makes a quick tap tempting, but that pressure is exactly what this trick counts on — press and hold before you tap, every time.

items.myth: An unlabelled USB stick found on the bridge is fine to plug in just to check who it belongs to.
items.fact: An unknown USB stick can install harmful software the moment it's plugged in — it is never your job to identify the owner yourself.
items.detail: Leave it unplugged and report it to the IT Service Desk directly, rather than asking around the crew mess first.

items.myth: A caller who sounds official and uses the right internal terms for the crew portal or IT systems is safe to give information to.
items.fact: A confident voice and familiar terminology prove nothing about who's really calling — the real IT Service Desk never asks for your password or a code over a call they made to you.
items.detail: Hang up and call back on a number you already trust, such as the one in the crew portal or your handbook, rather than continuing the call.

items.myth: A request for documents or funds from someone claiming to be a port agent or vessel manager is safe to act on quickly if it references your actual vessel and rotation.
items.fact: Referencing real details like your vessel name or rotation doesn't prove who's asking — that information isn't always private, and attackers use it specifically to sound credible.
items.detail: Passport and CDC scans go through the known secure agent portal, and port dues are never paid in gift cards — verify any such request through a channel you already trust.

items.myth: A short deadline to sign a Seafarer Employment Agreement (SEA) renewal, like 2 hours, is a real scheduling constraint you need to act on fast.
items.fact: A real SEA renewal is never so urgent that you have only a couple of hours to sign it — Crewing always leaves it waiting for you in the portal.
items.detail: Open the crew portal you already use directly, instead of any link in the message, to check your actual renewal status.
